title: Catégorie des types de mots [dont arbres plans] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: on the previous page Grothendieck sets up an equivalence. On one side are 'types de mots' of length n, meaning combinatorial patterns of words in letters such as u, u^{-1}, v. On the other side are isotopy classes of oriented disks D carrying a chord decomposition K, with a set S of n marked boundary points. He also defines a 'reduced order', with 'trivial' word types being those of reduced order 0.

This page gives a purely combinatorial counterpart.

The structure is a 'graphe segmenté avec involution': a linear graph (a segment subdivided into n consecutive edges, one per letter position) together with an involution sigma on the set of edges. Each 2-element orbit pairs two letter positions, like a letter and its inverse, or a chord joining two boundary arcs. Each fixed point is an unpaired letter.

Admissibility is defined by induction on the order n (the number of edges).
- Gamma is admissible if sigma = id.
- Otherwise, Gamma is admissible if some 2-element orbit epsilon of sigma consists of two consecutive edges, and the graph Gamma' obtained by contracting part of epsilon to a point is admissible, with the induced involution sigma'.
- Base case: every involutive graph of order 0 is admissible, hence also every one of order 1.

This is the familiar 'cancel an adjacent pair, then recurse' test.

The drawings show what is being encoded: disks whose boundary circle carries tick marks (the points of S, i.e. the letters), with pairwise non-crossing arcs and chords joining boundary arcs. One drawing places the boundary points on a straight segment with nested non-crossing arcs above it. Another shows a disk with a smaller disk attached by an edge, suggesting a tree of disks.

The intended theorem is that admissible means planar. If the contracted part is the union of both edges, the admissible (segment, involution) pairs are exactly the non-crossing partial matchings of n points on a segment, with fixed points allowed. These are counted by Motzkin numbers, and the perfect-matching case by Catalan numbers. Under this reading they correspond to the chord-decomposed disks of the previous page and to words that freely reduce by successive cancellation of adjacent paired letters.

The purpose is to build a combinatorial 'category of word types' equivalent to an isotopy category of disks with chords. Page 4 then passes to plane trees via cyclic orders at vertices (combinatorial maps), the dual picture.
errors: The text says Gamma' is obtained by contracting to one point 'l'une des deux arêtes' of the orbit. Read literally, only one edge disappears and the other becomes a fixed point of sigma'. That fixed edge then separates any enclosing pair, so a nested configuration like a b b' a' would not be admissible and the definition would capture only disjoint adjacent pairs. The drawings plainly show nested non-crossing arcs, so the intended operation is almost surely contracting the union of the two edges, or deleting the pair. Either the transcription should read 'la réunion des deux arêtes', or Grothendieck's sentence contains a slip.
No proof of the equivalence with chord-decomposed disks is given on this page. It is only a definition plus sketches.

ideas.what: Recursive characterization of planar (non-crossing) involutions on a linearly ordered set by successive contraction of adjacent paired elements
ideas.modern_name: non-crossing (partial) matchings; Motzkin/Dyck words; free reduction of words
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical combinatorics (Catalan/Motzkin numbers; Kreweras 1972 for non-crossing partitions)

ideas.what: Encoding words or word-types by disks with chord decompositions and marked boundary points (drawings), i.e. an isotopy-category model of word types
ideas.modern_name: chord diagrams / polygon dissections; planar diagrams and maps
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical (polygon dissections, Cayley, Kirkman); maps (Tutte, Cori)
ideas.where_published: Related in spirit to the dessins/maps discussion in Esquisse d'un programme (1984), but not this specific construction

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains a standard recursive definition of non-crossing pairings by adjacent cancellation, plus sketches of chord-decomposed disks. It is well-known combinatorics, interesting only as part of Grothendieck's 1980s work on plane trees and maps, and contains no new result.
transcription_corrections: 'contraction en 1 point de l'une des deux arêtes' is likely intended (or should be read) as contraction of the union / both edges of the orbit epsilon; at minimum this is mathematically required for the drawings' nested arcs to be admissible.

The marginal symbol transcribed as '\overset{\parallel}{1}_{0}' sits beside the big drawing near a boundary tick mark. It is probably a drawing label (e.g. a mark '1' / '0' or 'Io') rather than mathematical text.
'orbite^{ε/}' should be read as 'orbite ε de σ' (naming the orbit ε).
